kurz: How investment products that are neither shares nor funds are structured in legal terms, and who earns money from them.

bloecke.md:
With shares, bonds and fund units, the question of ownership is easy to answer. The shareholder is a co-owner, the bondholder has a claim against the debtor, and the fund unit represents a fraction of [[Segregated fund assets (Sondervermögen)|segregated fund assets (Sondervermögen)]], which do not form part of the insolvency estate if the fund management company becomes insolvent. All other securities that can be held in a securities account are structured differently in legal terms.

For each of these securities, it pays to clarify two questions. The first is who owns the money if the provider becomes insolvent. The second is what the repayment depends on and who designed that dependency.

bloecke.md:
## Bond basics

A bond is a loan in the form of a security. The issuer regularly pays a coupon on the face value and repays the face value at the end of the term. Coupon and yield are not the same thing. An investor who buys a bond with a 5% coupon at a price of 112 earns considerably less than 5%, because only 100 is paid back at the end. What matters is the yield to maturity.

The price moves in the opposite direction to market interest rates. If rates rise, the price of an older bond with a low coupon falls until its yield matches the new market conditions. The year 2022 is an example of this. The yield on ten-year German federal bonds (Bunds) rose by 274 basis points over the course of the year, from −0.21% to +2.53%.

The second component of the price is credit risk. The yield premium over a government bond with the same maturity is called the credit spread. It fluctuates far more than the default rates that actually occur. Duration, credit rating grades and bond ETFs are covered in the bond module. For this lesson, a brief overview is enough. A bond is a claim with a coupon and a repayment date. A certificate is also a claim, but it usually pays no fixed coupon, and the amount repaid depends on an underlying.

bloecke.unter: Normal, slightly rising shape. A maturity that is 28 years longer brings around 0.6 percentage points more yield.

bloecke.md: In economic terms, a certificate is an unsecured bond of the issuing bank whose repayment is linked to a formula. On the bond market, a bank pays a measurable premium for this credit risk. The buyer of a certificate bears the same risk but receives no coupon for it.

## Basic types of certificates

A certificate is a [[Bearer bond (Inhaberschuldverschreibung)|bearer bond]] under Section 793 BGB (Civil Code). The bank promises a payment at the end of the term, the amount of which it sets itself in the terms of issue. Four basic types cover most of the market.

An **index or participation certificate** tracks an underlying one to one. If it refers to a price index, the issuer keeps the dividends. Over a decade, this is the costliest difference from an ETF, and it appears in no cost disclosure.

A **discount certificate** is sold below the price of the underlying; in return, the gain is limited by a cap. In economic terms, it corresponds to the share without the dividend entitlement combined with a sold call option. The discount is made up of the option premium and the dividends retained by the issuer.

A **bonus certificate** pays a fixed bonus amount as long as the underlying never touches a barrier. If the barrier is touched, the bonus lapses, and the investor effectively holds the underlying, but without its dividends.

With an **express certificate**, the underlying is checked on annual observation dates to see whether it is above the starting level. If it is, the certificate is redeemed early together with a coupon. Otherwise it continues to run until the final observation, at which a barrier decides whether the capital is preserved.

In all these structures, the investor sells the bank a risk and receives a visible advantage in return, such as a discount, a bonus or a coupon. The bank's margin is contained in this exchange but is not shown separately.

When Lehman Brothers collapsed in September 2008, certificates issued by Lehman companies and sold in Germany also became practically worthless. They included products that had been marketed as capital-protected. Tens of thousands of private investors were affected.

In such a case, no protection scheme steps in. Statutory deposit protection covers balances of up to €100,000 per customer and institution, and at a bank also cash claims arising from securities transactions, but not securities. Statutory investor compensation (Anlegerentschädigung) reimburses 90%, up to a maximum of €20,000. It only pays out if an institution can no longer return securities held in custody or an investment firm fails to repay money owed from securities transactions, and not if an issuer fails to honour its own promise to pay.

A share costs €100 today, and the expected dividend next year is €3. A discount certificate with a cap of €100 and a term of twelve months costs €88. It repays the share price, but at most €100.

The maximum return is therefore (100 − 88) / 88 = 13.6%. Losses only arise below €88, that is after a price fall of 12%. Illustrative calculation excluding fees and taxes.

bloecke.unter: The kink at the cap comes from the sold call option. Below the cap, the product moves like the share; above it, the gain rises no further. The discount of €12 consists of €9 of option premium and €3 of retained dividend.

bloecke.md: At a share price of around €110.60, the certificate and the direct investment achieve the same return. Below that, the certificate is ahead; above it, the direct investment leads, and its lead grows with every further euro of price increase. A discount certificate is designed for a sideways movement. If you expect rising prices, it is the wrong product, all the more so the lower the cap.

## Warrants, knock-outs and time value

A **warrant** securitises an option, that is the right to acquire or deliver an underlying at a strike price. Its price consists of intrinsic value and time value. The time value depends on the remaining term and above all on the expected range of fluctuation, the implied volatility. The issuer sets this figure itself, because only the issuer quotes the price. An investor can therefore be right about the price and still lose money. This happens when the price rises as hoped but the issuer lowers the volatility it applies, so that the time value falls faster than the intrinsic value grows.

The price of a **knock-out certificate** contains almost no time value. The product has a strike price and a barrier. If the underlying touches the barrier, the product ends immediately. In the simple variants, the barrier is at the strike price, and the residual value is then zero. With open-end products, the strike price is shifted daily by the financing costs. The issuer finances the position, and an investor who holds for a long time pays this interest day by day through the adjusted strike price instead of through a disclosed fee.

The leverage comes from the small amount of capital needed for the same price movement; the investor does not take out a loan for it. Its level changes with the price. The closer the price moves to the barrier, the greater the leverage and the smaller the distance to a total loss.

The barrier is monitored during the trading hours of the underlying and not during the trading hours of the certificate. If, for example, news after the US market close is followed by an opening gap the next morning, the product has expired before a sell order could be executed. A stop-loss order of your own does not protect against this. It can only take effect once trading resumes, and by then the product no longer exists.

## CFDs and futures

A **CFD** is a contract with the broker on the difference between the opening and closing price and is not a security. It is not traded on an exchange and has neither an issuer nor an ISIN. The counterparty is the provider, which also quotes the prices. Since the ESMA product intervention measures, fixed limits have applied to retail clients in the EU, and BaFin (Federal Financial Supervisory Authority) has adopted them permanently in Germany. Leverage is limited to 30:1 for major currency pairs, 20:1 for gold and major indices, 5:1 for individual shares and 2:1 for crypto-assets. In addition, there is automatic closing out as soon as the margin has fallen to half, protection against a negative account balance and a mandatory warning stating the percentage of retail investor accounts that lose money. For most providers, this percentage is well above half.

A **futures contract** is the exchange-traded and regulated counterpart. It is a standardised forward contract on a derivatives exchange, where a clearing house steps in between the parties and eliminates the counterparty's default risk. In return, a futures contract entails an obligation to make additional payments (Nachschusspflicht). Losses are settled daily and can exceed the amount invested. The contracts are large. A DAX future moves €25 per index point, the mini version €5 and the micro version €1. Assuming an index level of 20,000 points, a single large contract corresponds to a notional value of €500,000.

bloecke.md:
## How issuers and distributors earn money

The issuer assembles a structured product from building blocks that it acquires on the market or hedges itself. Its income is the difference between the cost of the construction and the price at which it sells it. This margin is spread across several places: the initial charge during the subscription period, the gap between the bid and ask price during the term, the volatility applied, the financing rate of leveraged products and the dividends it collects as the hedging party.

In addition, there is the sales channel. If the issuer pays the selling bank a fee, this is an inducement that must be disclosed. These fees explain why the best-selling products are rarely the simplest.

Two documents make the costs verifiable. The [[Key information document (KID)|key information document (KID)]] under the PRIIPs Regulation summarises the risk indicator, scenarios and total costs on a few pages. The cost disclosure under MiFID II must show in euros, before the purchase and once a year thereafter, what the product costs, including inducements. Both documents are rarely read. Looking at them is particularly worthwhile when the product description sounds very attractive.

1. You should be able to calculate the repayment yourself and write it down in two lines. If that is not possible, the reason is a lack of understanding and not the complexity of the product.
2. The buyer should know which price path the product needs. A discount certificate needs a sideways movement, a bonus certificate an untouched barrier, a knock-out certificate a quick move in the expected direction. Without this knowledge, there is no well-founded expectation.
3. A comparison must include the simple alternative. Almost any structure can be approximated with the underlying and an instant-access savings account if the investor is patient. Only this comparison makes it possible to assess the structure.

Income from certificates, warrants, knock-outs, CFDs and futures is income from capital assets. It is subject to 25% capital income withholding tax (Kapitalertragsteuer) plus the solidarity surcharge and, where applicable, church tax. The former special restrictions on loss offsetting for derivative transactions (Termingeschäfte) have been abolished. Losses from share sales, on the other hand, may still only be offset against gains from share sales.

On Deutsche Börse, around 2,970 ETFs as well as 205 ETCs and 361 ETNs were listed in September 2026. A comparison is possible among these products. The certificate market is different, because new products with slightly shifted strike prices, barriers and terms are constantly being added. Two products with different barriers cannot be compared directly, and that makes price comparison harder.

With a fund, the investor bears the market risk; with a certificate, also the default risk of the issuing bank. With a leveraged product, there is the additional risk that the expected price movement occurs at the wrong time.

mitnehmen: Certificates, warrants and knock-outs are debt securities whose value also depends on the solvency of the issuing bank, and there is no deposit protection for them.

Every structure trades a visible advantage for a price scenario that the investor gives up; with a discount certificate, the discount consists of the premium for the upside sold and the retained dividends.
The costs rarely appear in the price list; they are contained in the bid-ask spread, in retained dividends, in the volatility applied and in the financing rate.
Futures carry an obligation to make additional payments; for CFDs, leverage limits, a forced close-out at 50% and negative balance protection apply to retail clients in the EU instead.
A product is only understood once its repayment formula can be written down in two lines.

begriffe.text: Security in which the issuer promises a payment to whoever holds it (Section 793 BGB). All certificates, warrants and knock-outs take this legal form. They securitise a claim against the issuer and are not segregated fund assets.
Risk that the issuer of a security fails to honour its promise to pay. It is ruled out for funds; for certificates, ETCs and ETNs it is always present.
Upper limit on the repayment of a certificate. Above the cap, the investor no longer participates in further price gains of the underlying. In return, the product is sold at a discount.
Price threshold at which a leveraged certificate ends immediately when touched. Monitoring is based on the trading hours of the underlying and not on those of the certificate.
Expected range of fluctuation of the underlying that is built into the price of an option product. It determines the time value and, for warrants, is set by the issuer itself.
Mandatory document under the PRIIPs Regulation for packaged investment products. On a few pages, it sets out the risk indicator, performance scenarios, total costs and the recommended holding period.
